narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Volkspele was the brainchild of Dr. SH Pellissier, who was inspired by Swedish folk traditions during a 1912 trip.
He introduced the first translated dances at a Boshof Sunday School picnic in 1914.
The movement expanded nationwide with the support of the Reddingsdaadbond, an organization created to assist Afrikaners after the Anglo-Boer War.

Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Volkspele is practiced at saamtrekke (gatherings) and during specialized educational weeks for students.
It functions as a cultural preservation tool and a means of social cohesion for the Afrikaner community.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by groups called laers.
It involves both singing and movement, categorized into 'folk-games'.
Participation is divided by age groups, with juniors in school and seniors out of school.
Watch for Volkspele.

narration: The tradition is closely tied to Afrikaanse Volksang (folk singing).

The sound is characterized by communal folk-singing in Afrikaans, originally adapted from Swedish melodies, performed during social 'folk-games'.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear volkspeledrag, based on 19th-century Voortrekker pioneer dress.
While the style is uniform nationwide, each laer uses specific colors for dresses and waistcoats, which are decorated with embroidered indigenous flowers.
on_screen: Images — MISSING

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dr. SH Pellissier is the founder and creator of the tradition.
Judith Pellissier, his wife, is the namesake of the training week for grade 5-7 pupils.
While the style of dress is standardized across South Africa, individual laers (local groups) are distinguished by their unique color schemes and floral embroidery.
The dance is a South African adaptation of Swedish folk-singing and folk-dancing traditions translated and introduced in the early 20th century.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.sound_description: The sound is characterized by communal folk-singing in Afrikaans, originally adapted from Swedish melodies, performed during social 'folk-games'.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Volkspele (South Africa). Vocal style: Folk-singing (Volksang). Form: Translated Swedish folk songs. Mood: communal, traditional, social. It should sound like this: The sound is characterized by communal folk-singing in Afrikaans, originally adapted from Swedish melodies, performed during social 'folk-games'. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
